title: Three Ways to Get Big Flavor with Less Meat: Dan Dan Mien, Braised Collards, Anchovy-Powered Pasta
summary: This ATK segment demonstrates how to extract deep flavor from a small amount of meat across three dishes. It starts with a Dan Dan Mien where ground pork is browned in a thin smear for maximum surface contact, then builds a concentrated chili-oil-based sauce with Sichuan aromatics and a dried-yacai accent. A second showcase braises ham hocks to create a lush pot liquor for braised collard greens, emphasizing long, gentle extraction of flavor and collagen. The third demonstrates a fast, high-umami pasta sauce built around anchovies, plus a parsley-basil pesto that doubles as an umami booster, finished with pasta water to emulsify and lightly coat angel hair. Throughout, the host highlights techniques for flavorful results from limited meat, including browning, tension between texture and flavor, layering of aromatics, and science-backed umami boosters.

title: Pasta Water Mastery: Emulsifying Sauces and Special Techniques with Lan Lam
summary: In this Techniquely episode with Lan Lam, viewers learn practical ways to use pasta cooking water to shape and finish sauces. The host demonstrates finishing sauce by allowing briefly cooked pasta to mingle with its sauce, then reintroducing reserve pasta water to rehydrate and emulsify, yielding a cohesive, glossy texture. He explores a classic Cacio e Pepe approach that uses toasted peppercorns, finely ground Pecorino Romano, and hot water to create a velvety emulsion, while also showcasing an oil-based tuna and capers sauce built through starch-rich cooking water and controlled heat to keep fats emulsified. The video emphasizes timing, texture cues (sheen vs. shininess), and temperature control to avoid over-softening pasta, with side notes on jarred sauce evaluation and other sauce-building ideas. Overall, it provides a practical, evidence-backed framework for using pasta water to adjust sauce consistency and mouthfeel across different sauce types.

title: Techniquely: Super Crunchy Buttermilk Fried Chicken — trim, brine, dredge + batter, fry at 340°F
summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely episode walks through a method to achieve an exceptionally crispy, craggy fried chicken crust by pairing a dredge with a buttermilk-based batter, preceded by careful trimming, strategic breast-halving for even cooking, and a flexible brining step. The host trims fat and extra skin, cuts breasts on a diagonal for even pieces, and brines the chicken with salt (plus optional sugar, garlic powder, and cayenne) for flavor and juiciness. The coating uses a flour-cornstarch base with baking powder, seasoned to echo the brine, plus a viscous buttermilk batter. Frying is conducted at 340°F in two batches with safety-minded techniques (low dipping height, singleton hands for handling batter, and per-piece temperature checks). The video emphasizes carryover cooking, advising pulling darker meat at 160°F and breasts at 140°F to finish in residual heat, resulting in juicy meat and a crust that stays intact without dragging or greasing-up. The host also notes practical workflow tips (pan choice for dredge, over‑shooting heat for recovery, and avoiding a doughy undercoat) and points viewers to the ATK app for the full recipe and Cook Mode guidance.

title: 3 Salting Methods for Better-Tasting Meats
summary: This video from America's Test Kitchen presents a practical, evidence-based look at three salt-application approaches for meat and fish: brining (salting in a saltwater solution), dry brining (salting directly on the surface and letting salt disperse into the meat), and seasoning (salting during cooking). title: Resting Meat: Carryover Cooking, Juices, and Rest Timings
summary: The video explains that resting meat after cooking is not idle but a crucial step because carryover cooking continues after removal from heat. It illuminates how a hotter surface compared with the interior drives a continued rise in the center, influenced by oven temperature and the size of the piece. Higher cooking temperatures and larger cuts can justify longer rests, while the surface-to-center temperature differential explains why finished doneness shifts during resting. A practical demonstration compares rested versus immediately sliced meat, showing reduced juice loss and improved juiciness—especially for chicken and pork—when rested. The host also contrasts methods such as searing followed by resting versus sous vide, noting that with a uniform water-bath cook there is little carryover and texture can differ. General resting guidelines are provided (turkey 30–45 minutes; roasts 15–20 minutes; steaks, chops, and chicken 5–10 minutes), along with caveats for when not to rest (e.g., tuna to preserve crust and a raw interior, or when a roast is overcooked and slicing helps the surface). The takeaway is a practical framework: use rest time to finish carryover cooking, retain juices, and plan service around the meat’s size, temperature, and cooking method.

title: Crispy Potatoes Without Deep Frying: Three No-Fry Techniques from Techniquely with Lan Lam
summary: This video explains the science of achieving crispy potatoes without deep frying and demonstrates three no-fry methods. Lan Lam contextualizes the idea that crispness comes from a dry starch network formed when water is driven off and heat and oil render that network into a browned, crunchy exterior. The three methods shown are: roasted smashed potatoes (steam-roasted, then smashed for maximum surface contact and browning), home fries pre-treated with an alkaline boil (baking soda in water to rough up exterior before roasting with aromatics), and oven fries coated with a cornstarch slurry (microwave-thickened slurry to build a protective shell, then steamed and browned). Each method emphasizes not cooking and crisping simultaneously, but sequencing steam, starch development, and browning to achieve a crispy, fluffy interior without deep frying.

It breaks down the three-part coating (flour, egg wash, breadcrumbs), explains how crumb size, type, and seasonings affect texture and flavor, and presents tweaks to boost crust integrity (Parmesan in crumbs for water resistance, egg-wash adjustments, batter-leaning approaches). The host then covers frying strategies tailored to meat thickness (shallow frying with a 2/3 oil depth, straight-sided pans), how to manage batter adhesion with a dry hand/wet hand method, and techniques to prevent crust collapse or cupping (perforating fat/silver skin, resting cuts on their side). The episode also shares methods for easier execution for those who fry infrequently, crumb-pressing tips, and finishing touches for each dish (schnitzel, tonkatsu, chicken parmesan) followed by a recap of how SBP can vary to distinguish similar fried dishes while maintaining crisp texture.

title: Pâte à Choux: The All-Purpose Dough for Profiteroles, Gougères, and Gnocchi
summary: This video presents pâte à choux as a universal, versatile dough that can be used for both sweet and savory dishes. The host walks through the classic double-cooking method: starting the paste on the stovetop, then binding it with eggs (emphasizing one-at-a-time addition and a food processor option to vent steam), and finally baking to produce crisp, hollow puffs. The demonstration covers practical technique for piping and shaping, plus several ready-to-plate variations: sweet profiteroles filled with ice cream and topped with chocolate, savory gougères with cayenne and Gruyère, and a gnocchi alla parisienne made from choux dough. Throughout, the video emphasizes steam-leavening (no commercial leaveners) and time/temperature control to achieve lift and crisp shells, with tips on batching, storing, and finishing sauces and fillings. All recipes and techniques are presented as ways to leverage one dough for multiple dishes.

title: Roast Two Chickens at Once: Hot-Pan Technique, Off-Oven Finish, and Schmaltz/Stock
summary: This ATK Techniquely episode demonstrates roasting two roughly 4-lb chickens in one batch using a preheated roasting pan and a finishing phase powered by residual oven heat. The host trims fat and skin to render cracklings, slides in slits to drain juices, seasons and trusses the birds, and roasts them on a hot pan without a rack. The technique emphasizes timing so the breast reaches 160–165°F while the thighs reach doneness via residual heat. After resting, the video shows carving both birds efficiently, collecting pan drippings to make stock, schmaltz, and gribenes, and then re-heating leftovers with steam and a brief skillet finish. It packs practical, repeatable steps for weeknight meals and emphasizes using the carcass remnants for flavorful stock and fat. There are also tips on utilizing pan drippings for dressings and flavoring other dishes.

title: Sous Vide Cooking: Essentials for Home Cooks
summary: America’s Test Kitchen’s Techniquely overview explains sous vide basics for home cooks, clarifying why the technique gained restaurant fame and how it translates to everyday cooking. The video also demonstrates a dramatic example: 72-hour short rib finished with a blowtorch, illustrating sous vide’s texture and uniformity potential, and points viewers toward further recipes and guidance such as Sous Vide for Everybody.

title: Butter-Washed Bourbon: Grated Butter Infusion and Two Flavor Outputs
summary: The video demonstrates a butter-based fat-wash technique inspired by bacon-wash, using grated butter to infuse bourbon and extract two products: bourbon-flavored butter and butter-flavored bourbon. The resulting infused liquids are then used in cocktails (notably Manhattan and Old Fashioned) and in a fall-inspired recipe (Autumn in New England) featuring sage, maple syrup, apple cider, and cider vinegar. The clip also suggests uses for the butter (hot honey as a compound butter, buttercream for cupcakes, or spreading on toast) and notes storage timelines for both the butter and the spirit, with a nod to Cook’s Illustrated as the source of the technique. The content addresses optional spirit substitutions (rye, rum, tequila) and invites viewer engagement in the comments.

title: Maximizing Spice Flavor: Layering Whole and Ground Spices with Time-Release Aromatics in Kima
summary: This Techniquely episode analyzes why when and how you add spices changes flavor, using a Kima (ground beef curry) as a through-line. Lan Lam explains that spices are not a single flavor but a blend of aromatic compounds with different volatilities, many of which are drawn out by heating. The video visualizes how aroma components separate in solution, contrasts whole versus ground spices in terms of surface area and release, and demonstrates a two-stage approach to spice addition: browning aromatics and infusing oil with whole spices for depth, then introducing ground spices later to preserve their more delicate notes. The segment also covers recipe scaling, a curry-blend ensemble analogy, and practical steps (browning onions, sautéing garlic/ginger, simmering tomatoes with yogurt, finishing with peas and cilantro) to achieve a cohesive, deeply flavored finished dish.

title: Water-Driven Browning: Onion Caramelization, Mushroom Searing, and Chicken Gravy
summary: In this Techniquely episode from America’s Test Kitchen, Lan Lam explains how adding water to the cooking surface can actually improve browning by using steam to regulate heat and promote Maillard and caramelization reactions. The transcript introduces two browning modalities—caramelization and Maillard browning—and explains why surface water keeps temperatures near 212°F, which can inhibit browning unless leveraged strategically. The video then demonstrates three water-assisted browning applications: caramelized onions cooked with a lid to trap steam for rapid wilting before browning; sautéed mushrooms that begin with a small amount of oil and a measured amount of water to generate steam and concentrate browning; and a chicken gravy built from browned stock where water extracts sugars and amino acids to support Maillard browning, followed by reduction and roux to finish the sauce. Throughout, the host references established techniques (Cook’s Illustrated) and Steve Dunn’s gravy method, and ends with tasting notes and prompts to apply the concept to other dishes.

title: The Foolproof Formula for Braising Beef (Catalan-Style Beef Stew) - Lan Lam
summary: This video presents a practical, four-part braising formula illustrated through a Catalan-style beef stew. Lan Lam demonstrates selecting a tough-cut (boneless short ribs), trimming fat, and cutting meat into 2-inch pieces before browning to form a deep fond. The braising liquid is built with aromatics (tomato, bay leaf, smoked paprika) and a liquid mix of water and wine, plus thyme and cinnamon, then the meat is braised in the oven at a low, steady simmer. The lesson emphasizes testing doneness by texture rather than relying solely on a thermometer, explains collagen breakdown as the driver of tenderness, and shows finishing the sauce with defatting, reduction, and a picata (toasted almond, bread, garlic, parsley) blend, optionally with sautéed oyster mushrooms, and final seasoning adjustments for balance. The video also contrasts oven braising as more foolproof than stovetop braising and reinforces the core idea: start with a tough cut, develop a flavorful braising liquid, cook until tender, and finish with a sauce that clings to the meat.

title: Side Fond: Bonus Flavor from the Sides of the Pot (Pork Ragù with Pappardelle)
summary: The video explains side fond, a flavor-building technique where browning and the Maillard reaction create flavorful browned bits on the sides of a pot. The host demonstrates how to set up ingredients (pancetta, pork shoulder, onion, fennel) and heat conditions to foster fond formation, then uses water and cream to dissolve and carry that fond into a braise. A 90-minute braise yields a juicy pork butt, and steam-condensation is used to scrape the fond off the sides without washing it away. The result is a richer sauce for ragù bianco with pappardelle, achieved without an extra searing step. The lesson covers when to add aromatics, the role of fat and collagen in tenderness, and why side fond can deepen flavor more efficiently by leveraging the pot’s side surface area.

title: Cold-Sear: A Fast, Dry-Heat Steak Sear Demonstration (Lan Lam, Techniquely)
summary: The video compares multiple steak-cooking philosophies, foregrounding a fast, low-mess method called cold-searing while also explaining traditional pan-sear, oven-finish, reverse-sear, and sous-vide approaches. Lan Lam contrasts the outcomes (edge-to-edge doneness with a rosy center vs. a gray ring) and details a step-by-step cold-sear process using a dry, hot non-stick skillet, a thick boneless steak, and careful heat management. Key practices include drying the surface, peppering before searing, avoiding pre-salt, heating to drive off surface moisture, flipping every two minutes to build multiple brown layers, reducing heat to finish cooking toward a 125°F center, a five-minute rest, and finishing with coarse salt for texture. The video also outlines the advantages and downsides of each method and notes how sous-vide and reverse-sear compare in precision and equipment needs.

title: Glazes That Stick: two-coat technique and thick, clingy glazes for meat and fish
summary: This ATK-Techniquely episode dissects glazes designed to stay put on proteins, showing how to build thick, clingy glazes that don’t melt away under heat. The host demonstrates a ketchup-based glaze for meatloaf and then pivots to two distinctive glaze approaches for pork chops and salmon: a gochujang–miso-based glaze for pork with a gentle cooking method, and a cornstarch-thickened salmon glaze built from a bold blend of vinegar, maple, soy, and liquid smoke. Key concepts include achieving a glossy, lacquer-like finish, the advantage of applying glaze in two coats, cooking meat at lower temperatures to preserve juiciness, and practical steps to prevent glaze from sliding off (half-coat first, avoid cross-contamination, broil for color). The episode also points viewers to additional salmon glazes and related recipes on AmericasTestKitchen.com and the ATK app.

title: Pan Sauces Demystified: Easy Vinegar-Pepper and Red-Wine Variants
summary: America's Test Kitchen presents a practical, technique-driven tour of pan sauces built from the fond left in the pan after searing protein. The video compares an easy flour-based version (using shallots, a touch of flour, chicken stock and pickle brine) with a more traditional red-wine pan sauce, and then highlights a butter-only finishing approach. Core concepts include: how to prepare and rest protein so the pan remains ready for sauce, how to deglaze and reduce to liberate fond, emulsifying cold butter into hot sauce to finish with richness, and recognizing when a sauce might break and how to rescue it. The demonstrated techniques are grounded in a specific recipe (vinegar-pepper pan sauce) developed for crispy-skin chicken, but the methods apply to a range of proteins that leave fond in the pan.

title: Decoding a Recipe: Anatomy, Prep, and Visual Cues (Sichuan Kung Pow Chicken)
summary: This Techniquely episode analyzes how well-tested recipes convey crucial information beyond the ingredient list, using Andrea Geary’s Sichuan Kung Pow Chicken as a running example. Lan Lam explains that headnotes and photos set the dish’s vibe and origin, while the ingredient list functions as both shopping and prep guidance. He emphasizes reading the recipe in full before cooking, spotting commas, parentheses, and keywords that signal timing and prep steps, and lining up equipment and ingredients for smooth execution. The demonstration highlights reading for visual cues and texture instead of relying solely on clock times, and shows a practical sequence including marinating considerations, toasting nuts and aromatics, cooking with a lid, and finishing the sauce to a glossy cling on the chicken. The video ends with reflections on active recipe reading and invites viewer engagement to improve success with any recipe.
